nameStory: The Common Mola gets its nickname 'ocean sunfish' from its habit of basking at the water's surface on sunny days, looking like a giant disk floating in the ocean. The name 'mola' comes from Latin meaning 'millstone,' referring to its round, flattened shape that resembles the circular grinding stones used in old mills.
description: The Common Mola is one of the most bizarre-looking fish you'll ever see - imagine a massive fish head with no tail! This enormous bony fish has a flattened, almost circular body that can grow as tall as it is long, reaching up to 6 feet in both directions. Adults typically weigh between 545 and 2,205 pounds, making them true ocean giants. Despite their intimidating size, these gentle giants are harmless to humans and feed primarily on jellyfish.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Unmistakably round and flattened from side to side, like a massive swimming pancake - there's truly nothing else like it in New England waters

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Tall dorsal and anal fins that extend dramatically up and down from the body, with no visible tail fin - the body just seems to end abruptly

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Absolutely massive - can be as wide as a small car and weigh more than a motorcycle, making them impossible to mistake for any other fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-brown to silvery coloration that appears mottled or blotchy, often with a slightly rough, sandpaper-like skin texture

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth positioned at the front of the head, appearing almost beak-like and seeming tiny compared to the fish's enormous body

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen floating motionless at the surface on calm, sunny days, sometimes lying on their side like a massive floating disk

habitat: Common Molas are found in New England's offshore waters, particularly in warmer months when ocean temperatures rise. They prefer open ocean environments and are most commonly spotted from boats in deeper waters beyond the continental shelf. These ocean wanderers follow warm currents and jellyfish blooms, occasionally venturing closer to shore in pursuit of their gelatinous prey.

seasonality.spring: Molas begin appearing in New England waters as ocean temperatures warm, though sightings are still relatively rare during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Mola sightings, when they're most commonly seen basking at the surface on calm, sunny days in offshore waters.
seasonality.fall: Still present in warmer offshore waters, though they may begin moving toward warmer southern waters as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters as they follow warm currents south or move to deeper, warmer waters.

funFact: A single female Mola can release up to 300 million eggs at once - more than any other known vertebrate! That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of the United States in tiny fish eggs.
confusionNotes: The Common Mola is so distinctive that it's nearly impossible to confuse with any other fish in New England waters - nothing else looks like a giant swimming pancake without a tail!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sunfish,' Common Molas are completely unrelated to the small freshwater sunfish like bluegills that many anglers know. The shared name is purely coincidental and refers to different families of fish entirely.
compareHints: The Common Mola is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in our region. While there are other species of molas worldwide, including the Southern Ocean Sunfish, the Common Mola is the only one regularly seen in North Atlantic waters. All molas share the distinctive tailless, flattened body shape, but the Common Mola is the most widespread and likely species encountered here.
